Yeah I'm not sure if I explained this well. When you video yourself with the front screen of the camera, you can detect your eye movement easily, but cant in the mirror?
Why can't you detect your own eye movement when looking in the mirror, but can when looking at yourself on let's say a phone screen (camera on in real time)?
There's a little delay induced while the camera captures and transmit the video on the screen.
Yeah, and this delay is crucial, because your eyes "video feed" is frozen while your eyes are in movement - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saccadic_masking

Even more mind-blowing when you realize that the brain knows when to "pause" the processing of the eyes streams.

Stare at something and move your head from the left to the right while keeping on staring. Eyes are moving to track the object you're staring at, but the brain doesn't "pause" the processing.

I think it pauses on focus changes - when you change the object you're looking at. More amazing is that it does track the object while you're moving your head. I don't think we do this "unconsciously", notice how hard it is to move your head and to keep looking straight in front of you. The eyes tend to target an object and stick with it until you find a new object, even up to the point that when you're twisting your head to the sides. Your eyes tend to fixate on objects and jump around between them, like some silly form of autoaim. This only stops working when you're spinning around - it stops working when the velocity gets high enough and at the same time motion blur kicks in.

It's fascinating when you think about it. Think how disorienting it would be to play a FPS that does this, yet we cope just fine in real life. I wonder if the VR guys ever though about this stuff.

This is because your eye in the mirror is capturing the view, whereas the camera on the phone is capturing the view. So on the phone your eye is looking at the screen, the camera is capturing the eye movement. Does that make sense?

Because when you're looking at your phone's video, you're seeing what the camera saw a fraction of a second ago. You see your eye move because the camera saw it.

When you're looking in a mirror, you're depending on your eyes only. Our eyesight 'freezes' for a fraction of a second when we move our eyes - IIRC it's to prevent motion sickness. You don't see your eye move in the mirror for the same reason it doesn't look like a panning shot when you focus your eyes in a different direction; focus goes from point A to point B, but not everything in between.
